title: Prospecting / ICP
brief_markdown:
Modules 2 and 3 gave you a story and the materials to carry it. This chapter is about who gets to hear it. The goal for the next two weeks: 50 to 100 accounts that have the exact pain in the narrative, with a named person at each, so that Module 5 has someone to write to.

### The availability trap
The most expensive mistake a founder-seller makes is choosing prospects by who is easy to reach instead of who has the problem. The accelerator cohort, the ex-colleague who now "does e-commerce", the friend with a Shopify store: all available, almost none of them run a TikTok Shop creator programme. A demo is about two hours of your week with prep and follow-up; twenty demos to people without the pain is a founder's week gone with no revenue at the end. The rare bad-fit account that buys anyway is worse: it never gets value, it churns, it asks for features that pull the product towards a customer you do not want, and it eats the support time your real customers should get.

Flip the picture. If Dana's team is losing a day a week to feedback rounds and someone she has never heard of messages her with a fix, she does not care that it was unsolicited. If your best friend runs a brand with no creators, nothing about the friendship makes it a sale. You will know you have an ICP when a friend says "oh, I could use that" and you ask two qualifying questions before you say yes.

### From narrative to characteristics
Module 2's narrative says who has the problem in prose. The ICP boils it down to metadata you can rattle off in one breath and that {{founder_2}} could check without {{founder_1}} in the room. For Myda it sounds like: "UK agency, 8 to 25 people, manages TikTok Shop for 10 or more brand clients, 2 to 3 in-house content people, 15 or more freelance creators, feedback goes out over WhatsApp and Slack, already pays for a creator-management tool." Every clause does a job. Ten clients and fifteen creators mean the video volume is high enough for feedback to hurt. Two or three content people mean a person whose week the feedback eats, and a seat count. Feedback over WhatsApp means they solve it with process today and know it fails. A paid creator tool means a budget line already exists.

The ICP describes an account, not a person. Myda has two segments and they are not the same animal: agencies (many brands, many creators; the pain is team time and client complaints) and brands (one catalogue, an affiliate or creator programme; the pain is hit-or-miss videos and winners nobody can reproduce). Write one profile per segment.

Two kinds of characteristics. **Required**: without them there is no deal. A brand with no creator programme has nothing for Myda to give feedback on, however large its TikTok Shop GMV. **Magnitude**: how much pain there is and how much they can buy: creators, videos per month, content people, countries. An account that clears every minimum is qualified; magnitude decides the order you call them in.

Some characteristics are visible from outside: headcount on LinkedIn, a live TikTok Shop storefront, affiliate links in creator bios, a partner-directory listing, a job post for a creator manager. Others you cannot see: how feedback actually reaches creators, whether anyone reviews a video before it goes live, what the UGC agency costs. Keep those in the ICP anyway and turn each into the question you ask in the first call. That is what this module's drill practises.

### Deer, not rabbits or elephants
Pain grows with size, but so does inertia. A one-person brand with five creators (a rabbit) says yes fast and churns fast, because there was never a process to improve. A global beauty group with an in-house studio (an elephant) has procurement and a UGC agency on an annual contract; win it and it owns your roadmap. Myda's deer: the 8-to-25-person agency, and the brand with one TikTok Shop manager and 50 to 200 affiliate creators. Enough pain to buy, small enough that the person on the call can say yes. Among deer, take the bigger ones: Dana with 12 clients and 20 creators beats an agency with 3 clients and 4 creators.

Geography: start where calls are easy. UK and German sellers are in your time zone and you can visit them; the US is the biggest market and a 9pm call. Fill the first list from UK and EU, keep US names on a second tab for Module 5.

### Scoring
Roll the characteristics into a score both of you can apply in thirty seconds, so a name {{founder_2}} adds on Tuesday is as good as one {{founder_1}} adds on Monday. Minimums first (all must be true), then points for magnitude, then a column for the trigger that says "now": a new TikTok Shop country launch, a job post for a creator manager, a founder posting about creator quality, an affiliate programme that just opened. Triggers go into the outreach message; that is why you capture them.

### Building the list
Pick one primary source per segment and stay with it until it runs dry. For agencies: LinkedIn Sales Navigator company search, marketing and advertising, 8 to 50 people, UK, DE, FR, keyword "TikTok Shop", then a people search for the titles inside those companies. For brands: TikTok Shop seller pages and the creator marketplaces are the directory; a brand with a storefront, an open affiliate programme and creator videos on the product page is announcing the pain in public. Partner directories and event attendee lists are secondary. Do not scatter across Reddit, Discord and X and call it prospecting. Do not buy a list: stale, thin, and you learn nothing from it. Build the first hundred by hand; the manual pass is where you discover that a characteristic you were sure about does not matter and another one does.

Capture metadata in columns from the first row: account, segment, country, headcount, brand clients or creator count, storefront link, one creator video link, trigger, score, contact name and title, email, potential intro. A column is a merge field. "I watched {creator_video} for {brand}; the hook starts at second four" is only possible if you recorded the link when you found the account.

### Who at the account
The contact is the person responsible for the pain who can pay to fix it. At an 8-to-25-person agency that is the founder or the head of content; the account manager feels the pain but does not own it. At a brand it is the Head of E-commerce or whoever the TikTok Shop manager reports to; the creator manager is a user, not a buyer, and the CMO is the complementary decision-maker you cascade to if the first door stays shut. Collect every relevant title at the account, decide after reading the profiles. Only then look for a warm way in: a shared 2nd-degree connection, or anyone at the company who can forward a note. Account first, relationship second.

Email is the channel you can template, track and follow up on, so find it: search, form it from the company's pattern, verify. If emails for this market are impossible to find, that is a go-to-market finding, better known now than in Module 5.

### This week
Monday, together: the two profiles, the titles, the disqualifiers, the score. Tuesday to Thursday, each founder: ten names a day from the primary source, scored, with trigger and creator video link in the row. Friday, together: prune anything that fails a disqualifier, find emails for the top twenty. Keep sending twenty LinkedIn requests a day, but from now on only to names on the list.

### What you build in this module
Together: the `icp` artifact. Two segment profiles with required and magnitude characteristics, the titles that own the problem and the budget, trigger events, disqualifiers, a fit score worked on Dana, Marcus and Sofia, the list-building recipe with a weekly quota per founder, the CRM columns and stages, and a 20-name starter list in which every row says why it fits. Module 5 writes to that list.

**Drill:** a 15-minute intro call with Dana, in which you qualify her against the ICP out loud and either book the real meeting with her head of content or park her with a reason.

build.spec_markdown:
Produce {{company}}'s ICP and prospect list, section by section, in this order. Work one question at a time; record each section with update_artifact as soon as it is good enough, then move on. Start from the company artifact's Narrative (who has it, how it is solved today, what it costs) and from the materials artifact (the merge fields its templates use are the columns the list must carry). Do not re-litigate the narrative here. The founders supply every company and person on the list from their own LinkedIn, TikTok Shop and directory research; never invent an account or a contact.

1. **Segment profiles.** Two: TikTok Shop agencies and TikTok Shop brands. For each, a one-breath profile, then a table of characteristics marked required (all must be true) or magnitude (more is better), each with a number or range: headcount, brand clients (agency) or creator-programme size (brand), creator videos per month, in-house content people, countries live on TikTok Shop, tools or agencies already paid for, how feedback reaches creators today. For every characteristic say where it is observable from outside, or write the discovery question that surfaces it on a call. Test every clause: does it signal the pain, the budget, or the ability to say yes? Delete clauses that signal none.
2. **Titles.** Per segment: the primary contact who owns the pain and the budget, the cascade (two or three further titles, in order), the complementary decision-maker to escalate to, and the user who is not a buyer. Write the exact LinkedIn title search string.
3. **Trigger events.** Five to eight observable events that mean "now" (new TikTok Shop country launch, job post for a TikTok Shop or creator manager, founder posting about creator quality, affiliate programme opened, new UGC agency hired, sudden jump in creator videos on a product page), with where each is observed and the line it earns in the outreach message.
4. **Disqualifiers.** Hard rules, starting from the company artifact's exclusions (freelancers, companies already contacted) and adding at least: brand with no creator or affiliate programme, agency with no TikTok Shop clients, not live on TikTok Shop in US/UK/EU, in-house studio that makes all video itself, enterprise with procurement, current beta tester or customer, agency that sells creator feedback as its own service. Every disqualifier must be checkable before the first message or by one question in the first call.
5. **Fit score.** A gate (the required characteristics, all true) plus points for magnitude and a point for a live trigger, applied in under thirty seconds, with the threshold to contact. Work it on three real examples from the persona files: Dana's agency, Marcus's brand, Sofia's brand. Say what each scores, whether it passes, and what the call should therefore be (full pitch, scoped beta, park).
6. **List-building recipe.** Per segment: the one primary source with the exact filter or query, two secondary sources, the fields captured per row, the owner (which founder works which segment), the time-box per day, and the weekly quota per founder in three numbers: names found, names that pass the score, contacts with a verified email. Geography order: UK and EU first, US on a second tab.
7. **CRM columns and stages.** The columns of the sheet (one per merge field the materials templates use, plus score, trigger, potential intro, stage, next step, next-step date, owner), the stage list with the rule for entering each stage, and the one standing rule that every row has a next step with a date.
8. **Starter list.** Twenty names the founders bring, at least eight per segment, in the table from the template. "Why it fits" must cite an observed fact and the trigger ("12 brand clients on the agency site, hiring a creator manager on LinkedIn since 14 Oct"), never "they sell on TikTok Shop".

Standards to enforce on every section: push back hard on "everyone selling on TikTok Shop" and on any profile a stranger could not check; a characteristic that is neither observable nor paired with a discovery question goes; no name on the list that fails a disqualifier; both founders could add a qualified name next week without asking the other. The whole artifact passes the stranger test: an agency owner or brand e-commerce lead who matches the profile would read it and say "yes, I have that problem". Mark the artifact done only when all eight sections exist, the score has been run on Dana, Marcus and Sofia, and the twenty rows each have a contact title, a trigger and a why-it-fits fact.

drill.channel: video call, 15-minute intro slot earned by a LinkedIn reply
drill.scenario: Dana answered your LinkedIn note with 'love it, let's definitely chat' and accepted a 15-minute intro call; she has another call straight after. You have the new ICP open. Use the call to qualify her out loud: ask the discovery questions from the artifact (brand clients, creators and videos per month, in-house content people, how feedback reaches creators today, what it costs her team, what she pays today, who decides), score her against the profile during the call and say what you concluded. She is warm and chatty, says 'love it' a lot, turns vague the moment money comes up, and offers 'let's definitely chat' instead of a date. End with either a booked 30-minute meeting with her and her head of content on a named day, or a polite park with the reason said out loud. Do not pitch for longer than a minute before the first question.
drill.buyer_opening: Hi! Sorry, two minutes late, it's back-to-back today. So I saw your note about creator feedback and honestly, love it, it's a constant thing here. I've got about fifteen minutes. Tell me a bit about what you're doing?

rows.criterion: Framed the call in the first two minutes: its purpose (find out whether {{company}} fits her agency), the 15 minutes, and that it ends with a decision on a next step; no pitch longer than a minute before the first question

Asked at least four of the ICP's discovery questions (brand clients, creators or videos per month, in-house content people, how feedback reaches creators today, countries) and got numbers back, not adjectives
Got Dana to put a cost on the problem in her own units (hours per week, re-shoots, client complaints) by asking, rather than asserting a cost at her
Asked how she solves it today and what she pays for it (tool, agency, freelancers, nothing) and held the question through her vagueness without apologising or dropping it
Asked who decides and who else needs to be in the room, and named {{company}}'s price or range when money came up, without flinching or discounting
Said the fit decision out loud on the call, citing two ICP characteristics she had confirmed ('you're exactly who we built this for because...' or 'I don't think we're the right fit yet because...')
Turned 'let's definitely chat' into a specific commitment: a named day, 30 minutes, her head of content attending, or a stated reason for parking; did not accept 'send me something' as the outcome
Finished inside 15 minutes, stayed warm when she got vague, and closed with a summary of what was agreed and the next step, in one or two sentences

rubric.below_threshold_note: Below 10: the discovery questions in section 1 of the icp artifact are not usable in a live call. Rewrite them as the exact words you would say, in order, and add a discovery question for every characteristic that is not observable from outside. Carry forward the weakest row. If Dana's answers contradicted the profile (for example she pays for no tool at all, or budget sits with a client), update the segment profile and the score before repeating with the same persona. Log the call in the CRM with stage and next step whether it was booked or parked.
